title: How to draft IEP goals faster on Mac: a teacher's routine for Pages and Google Docs
metaTitle: Draft IEP goals faster on Mac: a teacher's routine
description: Draft IEP goals faster on Mac with a reusable goal bank, a weekly progress table, and a checklist. Real numbers, sources, and what Lazur can do.
intro: To draft IEP goals faster, stop starting from a blank page. Keep a goal bank of reusable goal stems, and change only the parts that differ for each student. The routine below works on a Mac in Pages or Google Docs, and it keeps the legal requirements in view.
tldr: Build one goal bank in Pages or Google Docs and reuse it for every student.
Every annual goal needs a measurable target, a way to measure it, and a reporting schedule.
Start from your district's model form, not a blank file.
Write the measure before you write the goal wording.
Use AI or Writing Tools only for a first draft that you check against real data.

blocks.text: Teachers usually lose time in three places. The first is the blank page. The second is copying data into the right fields. The third is writing the same progress wording again each reporting period. You can fix all three with a few documents and a fixed routine. This page covers the numbers behind the problem, the fixes you can use today, and where Lazur helps.
Why drafting IEP goals takes so long

Start with the number people quote most. A 2002 federal study, the SPeNSE paperwork substudy, found that special education teachers spent an average of 5 hours a week on paperwork. The time varied by region. The study used a subsample of 972 special education teachers. It is old and self-reported, so treat it as a clue, not a measurement of your building.

A newer federal source points the same way, with a caveat. GAO's 2016 report, GAO-16-25, used focus groups in nine groups across 37 states. Educators in those groups estimated 1 to 2 hours a day on administrative tasks. GAO says the focus groups were not generalizable. Use the figure to see the pattern. Do not use it to predict your own week.

blocks.title: Old numbers, honest use
blocks.text: Quote these figures as background, not as a current district average. No current national survey tracks IEP paperwork hours. Say that plainly if your team asks for a number.
What drafting IEP goals costs you

Time is the first cost, and the easiest to measure. Take the 2002 figure at face value for a moment. Five hours a week over a 36-week school year is about 180 hours. That is my own arithmetic from the SPeNSE figure, not a study result. At the BLS May 2025 median of $67,170, based on a 2,080-hour work year, those hours equal roughly $5,800 of salary-equivalent time.

The second cost is staff turnover. Education Next, citing NCES data for the 2021-22 school year, reports that special education teachers were about 0.5 percentage points more likely to leave teaching than general education teachers. They were about 1 point more likely to change schools. Paperwork is one pressure among several. The data here do not isolate it.

Vacancies make the pressure worse. K-12 Dive reports that special education vacancies were about twice as likely as other teaching vacancies in 2021-22, citing IES. It also reports that 45 states reported special education teacher shortages in 2023-24, citing a Learning Policy Institute study. When a building is short, the paperwork lands on the teachers who stay.

The third cost is the goal itself. The law requires measurable annual goals. It also requires a statement of how progress will be measured and when reports go out (34 CFR 300.320). A goal that fails the measurable test is hard to report on. The next progress report takes longer, and the team may send the goal back for rewriting.
A vendor blog says paperwork can account for up to 50% of special educator time. It credits GAO's 2016 work without naming a specific study. Treat that as a secondhand claim, not a finding.
Mistakes that make the routine slower

items: Copying last year's goal and changing only the target, not the baseline.
Writing that a student will improve, with no target or criteria.
Keeping progress notes in email, then retyping them at report time.
Drafting a goal before you decide how you will measure it.
Pasting student names into a tool your district has not approved.

blocks.text: Each mistake costs time twice. You lose minutes while you write it, and you lose more when the team sends it back. The fixes in this page target these exact habits.
Why special education paperwork piles up

The structure is set by law. Every goal needs a measurable statement, a measure, and a report schedule. State and district forms often add fields on top. The result is the same structure written again for each student, while only the details change.

Data also sits in too many places. Progress lives in gradebooks, data sheets, sticky notes, and email threads. You then retype the same facts into the report. GAO notes that electronic reporting systems eased the burden, though some related strategies cost money.
Fixes you can use today without buying anything

The fixes below need no new software and no purchase. Each one targets a cause from the section above. Start with the goal bank, because it removes the blank page. Then add the measure step and the tracking table. Writing Tools and AI come last, after the content is right.
Build the goal bank in Pages or Google Docs

In Pages, choose a template, then go to Insert > Table. In Google Docs in your browser, use Insert > Table as well. Make four columns: Area, Goal stem, How you measure it, and When you report. Add one row for each goal you write often, such as reading, written expression, or behavior.

blocks.caption: Sample goal bank layout. Brackets mark the blanks you fill in for each student.
rows: By the end of the IEP year, given [text level], the student will read with [target] accuracy.
Oral reading probe scored by the teacher
Given a [prompt type], the student will write a [sentence type] with [target] correct elements.
When [trigger] occurs, the student will use [replacement skill] in [number] of [number] opportunities.
Weekly note in the tracking table

blocks.text: Start from the district model form, not a blank file. GAO notes that some states adopted Education's model forms, and many use them mainly as starting points for their own versions. In Google Docs, open the template, then use File > Make a copy. In Pages, open a copy with File > Duplicate. Keep the original untouched, so you always have a clean form to return to.
Write the measure before the goal

Most weak goals fail at the measure, not the wording. Decide how you will count the behavior before you write the sentence. Ask what you count, where you count it, how often, and who collects the data. If you cannot answer in one line, the goal is not ready. Then the wording gets easy.

items: Behavior: what the student does, in words someone can see or hear.
Condition: the materials, setting, or prompt the student gets.
Criteria: the target level the team agreed on.
Measure: the probe, sample, tally, or checklist you will use.
Schedule: when you report progress to the family.

blocks.text: Track progress each week so IEP progress reports take less time

Keep one tracking table for each caseload. After each session, add the date, the goal area, the data point, and a one-line note. At report time, read across the rows and write a short summary. You rebuild the report from real entries, not from memory.

Name files and tables by student code if your district allows it, not by full name. Save the file in the district-approved drive. Do not email the table to yourself as a workaround. That creates a copy outside the system your district gave you.
Writing Tools and AI for the first draft

Apple's Writing Tools guide, written for macOS 27, describes Proofread and Rewrite with Friendly, Professional, or Concise tones. Select the paragraph, then look for Writing Tools in the Edit menu or the right-click menu. Apple Intelligence is not available in every region or language, and usage limits may apply. If the tool is missing, Pages has spelling and grammar checks in its Edit menu.

A 2026 study by Waterfield and colleagues compared IEP goals written by teachers alone with goals written with ChatGPT. It found no statistically significant difference in quality ratings (p = 0.67). Qualitative findings were positive about easing workload. The study supports using AI for a first draft. It does not replace your check of each goal against the student's data.

blocks.title: Check student data rules first
blocks.text: EdWeek reports a privacy expert, Amelia Vance, warning of more breach points and possible AI bias, and asking for family disclosure and opt-outs. Follow your district's rules on student data before you paste anything into a tool.

Some teachers use a dedicated tool. MagicSchool's pricing page lists a Forever Free plan with 80+ teacher tools. Its Plus plan is $99.96 a year billed annually. The page lists FERPA and COPPA compliance across plans, but it does not name a separate IEP goal generator. Check the pricing page and your district's approval list before you sign up.
A worked example from vague goal to measurable goal

Here is a common before and after. Before: 'Student will improve reading.' That sentence has no condition, no target, no measure, and no schedule. After: 'Given grade-level passages read aloud, the student will read at [target] accuracy in [number] of [number] probes, measured with the teacher's probe log, reported each reporting period.' The second version takes longer to write. It takes much less time to report on.

Notice the brackets. They keep the structure fixed while the details change. Fill each bracket from the present levels statement and the team's decisions. Never fill a bracket with a guess, because a guessed target becomes a promise to the family.
Edge cases and what to do next

Some students need more than a goal bank. Behavior goals and goals for students with significant needs take longer to write well. Plan extra time for those, and do not force them into a standard stem. If your district bans AI tools, the goal bank and tracking table still work. If Writing Tools is unavailable in your region, use Pages' built-in spelling and grammar check.
GAO reports that Education's pilots for multi-year IEPs and paperwork waivers drew no state applicants. Do not wait for policy relief. Build the routine you can use this year.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app.

Lazur explains terms, points at fields, and drafts text that you review. It does not click buttons, edit files, or operate Pages or Google Docs for you. You still choose each goal, check the data, and decide what goes into the IEP. Lazur is not a plugin for either app, and it has no partnership with either maker.
There is a free trial with no credit card. Plans and their limits are on the [pricing page](/pricing). Check that page for current details before you decide.
Your next step this week

Start small. Build the goal bank with the goals you write most often, then copy the district model form. Add the tracking table before the next progress report is due. Each piece saves time on its own, and together they remove most of the blank-page work.

faq.question: How long does it take to draft one IEP goal?
faq.answer: No current study gives a reliable time per goal, so measure your own. Time a few drafts with a timer for one week. Compare that time with the weeks after you start the goal bank. Your numbers will tell you more than a national average.

faq.question: Can I use AI to draft IEP goals?
faq.answer: Only if your district allows it and you follow its data rules. A 2026 study found no statistically significant quality difference between teacher-only goals and goals written with ChatGPT (p = 0.67). Teachers stay the decision-makers. Check every goal against real data before it goes to the team.

faq.question: Does Apple have an IEP template for Pages?
faq.answer: No Apple-made IEP template turned up in the Pages guide. Pages starts every document from a template, so you can build your own goal bank table. Start from your district's model form if you have one.

faq.question: Does Writing Tools fix IEP wording?
faq.answer: Writing Tools can proofread a selection and rewrite it in a friendlier, more professional, or more concise tone. It does not know your student or your state's rules. Use it for wording only, after the content is right.

faq.question: Does Lazur read my student records?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer you and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your district's rules still decide what student information you can share with any tool.

faq.question: Do I need Lazur to draft IEP goals faster?
faq.answer: No. The goal bank, the model form, and the tracking table work in Pages or Google Docs without Lazur. Lazur can explain a term, point at a field, dictate notes, or draft a stem that you then check. It is optional.

costs.title: Hours that do not reach students
costs.text: The 2002 federal figure of 5 hours a week, applied across a school year, is roughly 180 hours. At the BLS median of $67,170, that time is worth about $5,800 in salary-equivalent terms. It is an illustration, not a district audit.

costs.title: Staff turnover and vacancies
costs.text: Special education teachers were about 0.5 percentage points more likely to leave teaching than general education teachers in 2021-22, per Education Next citing NCES. Special education vacancies were about twice as likely as other teaching vacancies in 2021-22, per K-12 Dive citing IES. Paperwork is one pressure, and the data do not isolate it.

costs.title: Goals that cannot be reported on
costs.text: The law requires measurable annual goals and a statement of how progress is measured (34 CFR 300.320). A vague goal is hard to report on, so the next progress report takes longer. The team may also send the goal back for rewriting.

costs.title: Privacy risk from shortcuts
costs.text: Pasting student details into an unapproved tool creates real risk. EdWeek reports a privacy expert warning of more breach points and possible AI bias, and asking for family disclosure and opt-outs. Follow your district's rules and your employer's rules on student data.

causes.title: The law sets a fixed structure
causes.text: Every IEP needs measurable annual goals, academic and functional. It also needs a way to measure progress and a schedule for periodic reports (34 CFR 300.320). Those parts repeat for every student, every year. Writing them from zero each time is where the hours go, because the structure never changes and only the details do.

causes.title: State and district rules add layers
causes.text: GAO found that state-imposed requirements add to the special education paperwork burden on top of federal rules. Your state form may ask for fields your district added later. Some states adopted Education's model forms, and many use them mainly as starting points. Every extra field is another place to type the same fact.

causes.title: Progress data lives in too many places
causes.text: Progress data sits in gradebooks, data sheets, sticky notes, and email threads. Then you retype it into the report. GAO notes that electronic reporting systems, launched in fall 2014, eased the burden. It also notes that some strategies cost money, so a district tool is not always free for you.

causes.title: Every student needs a different goal
causes.text: Copy and paste fails because goals must match each child's disability-related needs. A shared bank gives you structure. You still have to fit each goal to the child, the present levels, and the team's decisions. That fit is the real work, and it cannot be skipped.

causes.title: The workload is already full
causes.text: BLS describes special education teaching as potentially stressful, emotionally demanding, and physically draining. Outside instruction, teachers grade papers, update student records, and prepare lessons. Paperwork competes with all of that, so drafting often slides into the evening.

causes.title: Waiting for a policy fix
causes.text: GAO reports that Education's pilots for multi-year IEPs and paperwork waivers drew no state applicants. Relief from above is slow to arrive. The routine on this page works under current rules, and you can start it this week without a policy change.

fixes.title: Build a goal bank once
fixes.text: Make one document with goal stems grouped by area, such as reading, writing, math, communication, and behavior. Each stem has blanks for the baseline, target, measure, and schedule. SPeNSE found teachers spend less time writing IEPs when they choose from pre-developed lists of annual goals and update only what changes. In Pages or Google Docs, use Insert > Table.

fixes.title: Start from the district model form
fixes.text: Ask for the current district template and any state model form. GAO notes that many states use Education's model forms as starting points. In Google Docs, open the template, then use File > Make a copy. In Pages, open a copy with File > Duplicate, so the original stays clean.

fixes.title: Edit last year's goal, don't redraft
fixes.text: Pull the goal from last year's IEP, then change only what the new data supports. Update the baseline first, then the target. Keep the measure if the method still fits. This matches the SPeNSE finding that teachers do better when they update only the parts that need changes.

fixes.title: Decide the measure before the wording
fixes.text: Name the probe, sample, tally, or checklist before you write the goal sentence. Ask what you count, where you count it, how often, and who collects the data. If you cannot answer in one line, the goal is not ready. The wording is then the easy part.

fixes.title: Track progress each week in one table
fixes.text: Keep one table per caseload. After each session, add the date, the goal area, the data point, and a one-line note. At report time, read across the rows and write a summary. You rebuild nothing from memory, and the report draws on real entries.

fixes.title: Use Writing Tools after the content is right
fixes.text: Apple's Writing Tools can proofread selected text and rewrite it in Friendly, Professional, or Concise tones, according to Apple's macOS 27 guide. Look for Writing Tools in the Edit menu or the right-click menu. Apple Intelligence is not available in all regions or languages, and usage limits may apply.

fixes.title: Draft with AI, then check every goal
fixes.text: A 2026 study by Waterfield and colleagues found no statistically significant difference in quality ratings between teacher-only goals and goals written with ChatGPT (p = 0.67). The study supports a first draft. It does not replace checking each goal against the student's data and the team's decisions.

fixes.title: Dictate notes first, then edit
fixes.text: Talk through the student's progress before you type. Hold fn in any app and speak. Dictation types clean, formatted text at the cursor. Then edit the draft against the data. Test a spoken first pass on one goal before you rely on it.

fixes.title: Get one colleague to read a goal aloud
fixes.text: Read the goal out loud to a colleague who knows the student. If they cannot picture how you will measure the behavior, rewrite the measure. This check takes less time than a rewrite after the meeting.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the goal bank
plan.text: Open a new Pages or Google Docs file. Make a table with four columns: Area, Goal stem, How you measure it, and When you report. Add the goals you write most often, with blanks for the baseline and target.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Copy the district model form
plan.text: Start from the current district template, not a blank file. Save a copy so the original stays clean. Map each form field to a row in your goal bank.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Draft three goals with the checklist
plan.text: Use the behavior, condition, criteria, measure, and schedule checklist for each goal. Write the measure first. Then write the sentence around it.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set up the progress table
plan.text: Create one tracking table for your caseload. After each session, add the date, goal area, data point, and a one-line note. Keep it in the district-approved drive.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review and check
plan.text: Read each goal aloud. Compare it to the present levels statement and the data. Use Writing Tools to proofread only after the content is right.
